patients.label: 51-year-old female with acute cerebellar infarcts treated surgically and followed through ICU, inpatient and outpatient rehabilitation

identity_evidence.quote: A 51-year-old healthy female arrived at the emergency center

attribution_limitations: The abstract states acute bilateral cerebellar infarcts, while the case text documents left cerebellar ischemia on the repeat CT and left-sided surgery; bilateral involvement is not otherwise described in the case text. Parent decision: two values for one attribute (infarct laterality) is a source conflict; the bilateral (p1-f020) and left (p1-f019) condition items are both review_only, while the unlateralized cerebellar CVA diagnosis and the dated CT results stay included.

The Figure 1 caption places the MRI two months after a "left occipital craniotomy", whereas the case text describes a left suboccipital craniotomy; the caption does not say they are different operations.
Physical therapy is said to have been initiated 30 days after the initial fall and eight days after OT was initiated, but OT was evaluated three days after the fall; the two intervals do not add up.

The Discussion states the patient had an absence of serious medical complications post-surgically, whereas the case text and abstract describe postoperative hemorrhages and hydrocephalus. Parent decision: the Discussion sentence is author interpretation and is not recorded as an absent-complication item; the imaging-documented hemorrhages and hydrocephalus stay included.

Outpatient duration is stated as 41 weeks of rehabilitation, while the figure captions label outpatient weeks 17-56 and Table 3 labels the final testing row "Discharge - 10.5 months"; outpatient therapy also ends around month ten in the text.

Table 2 prints a colspan marker around the Month 1 header and the Month 2 data cell. Cells were read by position (Outpatient evaluation, then Month 1 to Month 9); the Month 1 and Month 2 assignments follow that position and the merged cell may span both months. Parent check of the raw XML: the header row spans Month 1 over two grid columns and each body row spans its third value over two columns, offset by one; there are ten printed values for ten time labels, so the positional reading (third value = Month 2) is kept, but that cell also overlaps the second Month 1 column.

Table 3 prints N/A for all hand tests at 6 months and for the Box and Block Test at the outpatient evaluation and 1 month; the source does not define whether N/A means not applicable or not performed.

The text cites Figure 8 for wheelchair propulsion with moderate assistance, but the Figure 8 caption describes a seated rest break during gait training with a rolling walker and ceiling-mounted harness.

Final function is described as ambulating and standing with assistance and performing most ADL with standby or set-up assistance (abstract), requiring support and supervision at home (results), and being independent in modified ADL and instrumental ADL (conclusion). Parent decision: the abstract (14 months) and results (month ten) statements are different time points and stay included; the untimed conclusion claim of independence in modified and instrumental ADL contradicts the supervision described in the results and is review_only.
The abstract phrase "ambulate, and stand with assistance" does not make clear whether "with assistance" also qualifies ambulation.
The social history says she was a former smoker for eight years, which can mean eight years of smoking or eight years since quitting.
Table 3 states units in kg for hand grip, Three Jaw Chuck, Two point and Lateral Pinch, but does not say what the Two point test measures.
Wheelchair propulsion at week seven of IPR is reported as 50 feet in the OT section and as 24 m (80 ft) in the PT section; the source does not identify them as the same measurement.
The Figure 9 caption calls the meal preparation independent, whereas the text that cites Figure 9 describes simple meal preparation with close supervision.

evidence.quote: The majority of the ICU OT treatment sessions consisted of MSS, which is an application of a series of sensory techniques that are customized in occurrence and amount in order to increase arousal and awareness to elicit a purposeful behavior.

The patient initially responded to the MSS with an elevated heart rate and blood pressure, and then began communicating by nodding and biting on her endotracheal tube, turning her head away, and wiggling her fingers.
Subsequent OT treatments in the ICU included bed mobility and ADL retraining for which the patient was initially dependent.

As the patient became more responsive, neuromuscular re-education techniques were used such as the therapist placing the patient’s right hand on her hair and asking her to lower her arm to touch her eyes, nose and mouth, use of a universal cuff on the right upper extremity to assist with brushing her teeth and preparing to eat.

items.name: Core strength and stability, lower extremity strengthening, gait training with the U-step with minimal assistance from family, and wheelchair self-propulsion

items.subject: index_patient

time.text: Even after discharge from outpatient PT/OT

evidence.quote: Even after discharge from outpatient PT/OT, the patient’s spouse set up an unweighting harness for her home treadmill by installing asupport system in the ceiling of their living room.

items.name: Unweighting harness support system installed by the spouse in the ceiling of the living room for her home treadmill

items.subject: index_patient

evidence.quote: After discharge from IPR, outpatient OT was initiated which included a vision rehabilitation component and employing a transparent central field patch to facilitate scanning and ambient light.

items.name: Transparent central field patch to facilitate scanning and ambient light

items.subject: index_patient

time.text: two months after left occipital craniotomy

evidence.quote: Brain MRI (T2 Weighted) without gadolinium completed two months after left occipital craniotomy and evacuation of infarcted left cerebellar tissue. Images demonstrate left cerebellar subacute and chronic infarctions as well as an area of acute infarction within the pons.

items.name: Brain MRI (T2 weighted) without gadolinium
items.finding: Left cerebellar subacute and chronic infarctions and an area of acute infarction within the pons

evidence.quote: A head computerized tomography (CT) demonstrated that there was no acute intracranial event.
She was bradycardic at 25 to 39 beats per minute.

items.subject: index_patient

evidence.quote: The next day a repeat head CT demonstrated acute ischemia of the left cerebellum mainly in the PICA distribution.

items.name: Repeat head CT
items.text_value: Acute ischemia of the left cerebellum mainly in the PICA distribution

items.subject: index_patient

evidence.quote: A head CT revealed hydrocephalus with dilation of the lateral ventricles including temporal horns and third ventricle, along with fourth ventricle compression and brain stem compression due to edema of a left cerebellar infarct.

items.name: Head CT after the fall
items.text_value: Hydrocephalus with dilation of the lateral ventricles including temporal horns and third ventricle, fourth ventricle compression and brain stem compression due to edema of a left cerebellar infarct

items.subject: index_patient

evidence.quote: After surgery, a head CT demonstrated a new hemorrhage and gas within the operative cavity along with an increased mass effect on the left side of the fourth ventricle which was completely effaced with moderate obstructive hydrocephalus.

items.name: Head CT after surgery
items.text_value: New hemorrhage and gas within the operative cavity, increased mass effect on the left side of the fourth ventricle which was completely effaced, moderate obstructive hydrocephalus

evidence.quote: The patient’s intracranial pressure (ICP) was found to be elevated and she had an external ventricular drain (EVD) placed for therapeutic drainage of her cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).

evidence.quote: She was able to perform a five-times-sit-to-stand test in 33 seconds with minimum assistance in the parallel bars.

items.name: Five-times-sit-to-stand test

claims.text: A 51-year-old previously healthy, athletic female with a patent foramen ovale, two superficial venous thrombi and a history of depression presented with acute dizziness, severe headache, diaphoresis, photophobia, nausea and emesis after being unable to lift herself during pushups. An initial head CT showed no acute intracranial event, symptoms were first believed vasovagal, and she was bradycardic at 25 to 39 beats per minute.

evidence.quote: A 51-year-old healthy female arrived
Her health history included a patent foramen ovale, two superficial venous thrombi, and a history of depression.
presenting with acute dizziness, a severe headache, diaphoresis, diffuse photophobia, nausea, and emesis
The patient reported that she had been doing pushups during a televised total body workout and was suddenly unable to lift herself up.
A head computerized tomography (CT) demonstrated that there was no acute intracranial event.
Her symptoms were initially believed to be a vasovagal reaction.
She was bradycardic at 25 to 39 beats per minute.
Finally, the patient was a high-level athlete prior to her injury and the patient translated this work ethic and response to adversity in her recovery.

claims.text: A repeat head CT the next day showed acute left cerebellar ischemia in the PICA distribution and she was admitted with an acute cerebellar CVA, with an initial NIHSS score of three and modified Rankin score of 2/6. Four days after admission she was found face down in the bathroom, and head CT showed hydrocephalus with fourth ventricle and brain stem compression due to edema of a left cerebellar infarct.

evidence.quote: The next day a repeat head CT demonstrated acute ischemia of the left cerebellum mainly in the PICA distribution.
Upon this finding, the patient was admitted into the hospital diagnosed with an acute cerebrovascular accident (CVA) in the cerebellum.
She demonstrated an initial score of three on the National Institute of Health Stroke Scale and was placed on the hospital stroke protocol.
The patient scored a 2/6 (0=no impairment, 6=severe disability/bedridden) on the modified Rankin scale.
Four days after her admission, she was found face down in bathroom after ambulating there independently.

A head CT revealed hydrocephalus with dilation of the lateral ventricles including temporal horns and third ventricle, along with fourth ventricle compression and brain stem compression due to edema of a left cerebellar infarct.

claims.text: She was moved to the ICU for emergency left suboccipital craniotomy with removal of infarcted cerebellar areas, followed by a right frontal ventriculostomy, posterior fossa decompression, an external ventricular drain and reopening of the craniotomy for clot evacuation after new hemorrhages. Judged to have a poor prognosis, she received a palliative care consultation and a tracheostomy, and was moved to a tracheostomy collar with supplemental oxygen.

evidence.quote: The patient was then transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU) and had emergency surgery for a left suboccipital craniotomy with removal of the infarcted areas in the cerebellum.

After surgery, a head CT demonstrated a new hemorrhage and gas within the operative cavity along with an increased mass effect on the left side of the fourth ventricle which was completely effaced with moderate obstructive hydrocephalus.
The patient had postoperative hemorrhages and hydrocephalus and was deemed to have a poor prognosis.
Later in the day the patient demonstrated a reduced level of consciousness and was taken to the operating room again where a right frontal ventriculostomy was performed to decrease the hydrocephalus.
She subsequently had a posterior fossa decompression and she was deemed to have an overall poor prognosis.
The patient’s intracranial pressure (ICP) was found to be elevated and she had an external ventricular drain (EVD) placed for therapeutic drainage of her cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
She subsequently developed a hemorrhage surrounding her EVD in the right frontal lobe and a hemorrhage within the right lateral ventricle.
The next day she underwent surgery to reopen her suboccipital craniotomy for evacuation of a clot.
In light of her poor prognosis, the patient received a palliative care consultation to assist in coordinating care and decision making 11 days after her fall and surgery.
Twelve days after her initial fall, a tracheostomy was completed and she remained on ventilator support.
Two days after the tracheostomy, she was successfully transferred to supplemental oxygen at 28% FiO_(2) via a tracheostomy collar.

claims.text: During about six weeks in the ICU, OT began with multimodal sensory stimulation and PT with early mobility and tilt-table work. After about 10 weeks of inpatient rehabilitation, with gains in sitting balance, transfers, wheelchair propulsion and gait training using unweighting systems, she was discharged home with moderate assistance from her husband, a wheelchair, platform walker, shower chair and tub transfer bench.

evidence.quote: The patient underwent a total of 14 months of PT and OT – six weeks in the intensive Care Unit (ICU), approximately 10 weeks in Inpatient Rehabilitation (IPR), and 41 weeks of outpatient rehabilitation.

The majority of the ICU OT treatment sessions consisted of MSS, which is an application of a series of sensory techniques that are customized in occurrence and amount in order to increase arousal and awareness to elicit a purposeful behavior.
Occupational therapy evaluation, interventions and outcomes: Three days after the initial fall and surgery, the patient was evaluated by OT.
Physical therapy evaluation, interventions and outcomes: Physical therapy treatments were initiated 30 days after the patient’s initial fall and eight days after OT was initiated in the ICU.
At the end of her ICU stay (or after a week-and-a-half of treatment) she was able to tolerate a 70 degree tilt-table angle for 45 to 55 minutes three times per day.
The patient was directly admitted to the IPR unit after a six week ICU stay.
During inpatient rehabilitation, the patient received a total of 54 visits of OT, 51 visits of PT, 47 visits of SLP and 22 visits of recreation therapy.
The patient demonstrated static sitting balance of 40 seconds with steadying assist.
The LiteGait for gait training continued to be emphasized and the patient was able to ambulate 426 m (1400 ft) with 0-11 kg (0-25 lbs) of unweighting at 0.22-0.27 m/s (0.5-0.6 mph).
She was able to perform a five-times-sit-to-stand test in 33 seconds with minimum assistance in the parallel bars.
By week 10, the patient could perform daily bathing, grooming, showering, and functional mobility tasks with moderate assistance from her husband without cues from the therapists.

Home adaptations included a wheelchair ramp and was discharged to home with a wheelchair, platform walker, shower chair, tub transfer bench and subsequently received outpatient PT and OT after a one week gap in treatment due to the holidays.
This allowed for safe discharge to her adapted home environment.

claims.text: Outpatient PT and OT lasted 41 weeks, starting with whole body ataxia, weakness, a PEG tube and left eye patching, and PSFS, hand function, PASS, Berg and Timed Up and Go measures were tracked. By month ten she plateaued and functioned at the wheelchair level with family supervision; at 14 months she lived at home with her husband, could ambulate and stand with assistance, and performed most ADL with standby or set-up assistance.

evidence.quote: During outpatient rehabilitation, the patient received a total of 117 visits of OT, 115 visits of PT, and 110 visits of SLP over 41 weeks of rehabilitation.
She displayed whole body ataxia as well as bilateral upper and lower extremity weakness with the left side weaker than the right.
The patient relied on a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube for nutrition due to risk of aspiration and received patching of the left eye to address her double vision and left eye palsy.
Upon initial evaluation, the patient’s Postural Assessment for Stroke Scale (PASS) score was 11/36 (0= maximal disability, 36= no disability).
After one month, her PASS score was 26/36.
At four months, her PASS score was 28/36 and was not repeated after this date.

At the beginning of month five, the patient’s Berg balance score was 13/56 (56 = normal balance) and by the end of the sixth month, it had improved to 17/56 and was no longer reported in the medical record.
By month ten, the patient had started to plateau with her functional level and was being prepared for discharge.

Fourteen months after the initial infarcts, the patient was able to reside in her own home with her husband, ambulate, and stand with assistance and perform most activities of daily living with standby or set-up assistance.

She continued to require support and supervision at home from family and hired assistance to ensure safety although she was able to function in her environment at the wheelchair level with little to no assistance.

Her initial series of OT visits emphasized control of upright sitting with cueing as well as utilizing kinesiology tape to facilitate cervical extension.
The patient participated in upper extremity ROM progressing from gravity-eliminated/AAROM and also received scapular mobilizations.

Vision treatments included application of tactile and auditory stimulation for coordination of eye active range of motion (AROM) and a trial of clear eyeglasses with a unilateral gauze patch over the right eye for diplopia.
The patient also performed gaze stabilization exercises as well as progressive transfer activities incorporating tracking and planning.

During week seven and eight in IPR, specific treatments included emphasizing wheelchair seating and positioning with tasks such as leaning forward in her wheelchair to rest her elbows on tops of her thighs and returning to upright as well as wheelchair push-ups and lower body dressing.
Vision treatments included activities such as visual fixation on targets with lateral head movements, letter and number reading, and utilization of the Nintendo Wii emphasizing hand-eye coordination.

By week nine, OT treatments emphasized reaching forward and down to the ground while in a wheelchair with return and upper extremity stretching and strengthening focusing on optimizing functional reaching activities.

The initial series of lower extremity exercises were AAROM and as the patient progressed to tolerating increased weightbearing and upright activity, open chain activities were modified to be performed in closed chain in varying planes of movement.

Upon week two, the patient received assistance with standing activities while using a standing frame and SARA Plus mechanical standing unit (ArjoHuntleigh, Addison, IL http://www.arjohuntleigh.us/) for assisted pre-gait activity with moderate assistance.
By week two, the patient was tolerating light ankle weights of one pound for long arc quads and progressing to active range of motion from active-assistive.

Throughout the treatment sequence, the patient was assisted in use of a recumbent elliptical machine; this initially focused on the lower extremities but as the patient’s grasp improved, upper extremities were also incorporated.
The patient also transitioned to using a mechanical ceiling-mounted gait harness and was able to tolerate ambulation over 18 m (60 ft) with maximum assistance of two people.

By week four of PT in IPR, the patient had progressed to gait training activities utilizing the LiteGait assisted gait system (LiteGait, Tempe AZ, http://www.litegait.com/) and the patient was able to support 60-90% of her body weight with 4.5-8 kg (10-40 lbs) of assistance from the harness for 92 m (301 ft) on even surfaces.
She began unsupported gait training with a platform walker and bilateral hand splints but required two seated rest breaks over 60 m (190 ft).
The patient was also able to begin car transfer training with moderate to maximum assistance.

The patient’s therapeutic exercise had subsequently progressed to standing heel and toe raises, marching, mini-squats, ankle pumps, seated alternating hip flexion, supine bridging and balance and core strengthening activities while reaching outside of her base of support.

Home adaptations included a wheelchair ramp and was discharged to home with a wheelchair, platform walker, shower chair, tub transfer bench and subsequently received outpatient PT and OT after a one week gap in treatment due to the holidays.

Upon initiation of outpatient PT and OT seventeen weeks after her fall and craniotomy surgery, the patient presented with decreased core strength requiring a specialized wheelchair for positioning and stability.
The patient relied on a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube for nutrition due to risk of aspiration and received patching of the left eye to address her double vision and left eye palsy.
The patient relied on a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube for nutrition due to risk of aspiration and received patching of the left eye to address her double vision and left eye palsy.

It should be noted that in IPR the patient's right eye was patched as her right eye dysfunction was limiting her performance on functional retraining but in outpatient occupational therapy, retraining the visual musculature could be emphasized and the patch was switched to the left eye.

Her OT intervention initially focused on family education for home exercise program (HEP), core stability activities while laying supine on a mat with moderate to maximal assist, and unsupported sitting with moderate assistance.
Scapular mobilization and kinesiology taping was utilized to encourage upright posture as well as to facilitate normalized motion of both arms.

Monocular visual perception activities and tracking activities were utilized in conjunction with taping to the central portion of the patient’s left glasses lens to allow for continued peripheral vision and light input.

By the second month, fine motor coordination (FMC) activities were initiated utilizing large sized pegs and beads requiring hand-over-hand assistance for fine motor tasks to facilitate normalized movement patterns secondary to ataxia (Table 3).
Interventions also focused on modified ADL tasks with an emphasis on weight bearing through alternating upper extremities to incorporate into HEP.

Neuromuscular re-education with weight bearing and proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation (PNF) D1/D2 patterns were completed while sitting at the edge of the mat with minimal to moderate assistance to avoid loss of balance.

During the third month, a resisted upper extremity exercise program was initiated with medium resistance elastic band with scapular retraction and shoulder horizontal abduction/adduction with trunk rotation to strengthen her core.
She also participated in standing level neuromuscular re-education activities and gross motor coordination (GMC) tasks.

Core strengthening interventions included quadruped positioning on the mat with alternating arm-and-leg-lifts with minimal assistance as well as neuromuscular re-education techniques while seated on a foam pad reaching outside her base of support with minimal assistance to maintain balance.
In addition, the patient performed light resistance clothespins and therapeutic putty to improve hand strength and dexterity.

The patient was introduced to modified techniques for dressing in supine as well as adaptive equipment for self-feeding as she was now able to eat with a modified diet and no longer required a feeding tube.

Due to her continued need for a wheelchair for mobility, during months seven and eight, she received instruction in adaptation of kitchen and laundry tasks at the wheelchair level with emphasis on safety and adapted performance.
She also started a writing program with her non-dominant left hand as coordination was improving faster than her right hand.

Through months nine and ten, interventions continued to focus on modified techniques and safety with both basic and advanced ADLs as well as functional transfers and independence at wheelchair level in preparation for discharge.
Interventions for physical therapy focused on dynamic and static sitting and standing balance activities, pre-gait and family education.
Therapeutic activities included unsupported trunk rotation with weighted ball and seated marching with alternating upper extremity requiring moderate assistance for support and upright posture.
Months two and three focused on core stability exercises in supine and quadruped via crawling forward and backward, supine-to-kneeling and mini push-ups with moderate assistance.

Pre-gait in the parallel bars was advanced to incorporate single leg stance, step tap with alternating lower extremities in both the ascending and descending direction; her anterior step-downs and posterior step-ups with external perturbations required moderate to maximal assistance for fall prevention.

As her core stability increased in months five and six and she was no longer falling forward during transitional movements, her gait training progressed to outdoor, uneven surfaces, and stair training.
More advanced strengthening and balance activities were initiated including lunges, squats, standing ball bouncing and tandem weight shift with minimal assistance to maintain balance.
She was also started on a program with the LiteGait and treadmill as well as an elliptical machine.
By month seven, the patient was started on a U-step walker (In-Step Mobility Products, Skokie, IL, 60076. www.ustep.com) to aid in ambulatory control and balance.
Transfer training shifted focus toward family education and safety to prevent falls.

Months eight through ten focused on core strength and stability, lower extremity strengthening, gait training with the U-step with minimal assistance from family, and independence at wheelchair level with self-propulsion.
Even after discharge from outpatient PT/OT, the patient’s spouse set up an unweighting harness for her home treadmill by installing asupport system in the ceiling of their living room.
After discharge from IPR, outpatient OT was initiated which included a vision rehabilitation component and employing a transparent central field patch to facilitate scanning and ambient light.

Brain MRI (T2 Weighted) without gadolinium completed two months after left occipital craniotomy and evacuation of infarcted left cerebellar tissue. Images demonstrate left cerebellar subacute and chronic infarctions as well as an area of acute infarction within the pons.
A head computerized tomography (CT) demonstrated that there was no acute intracranial event.
She was bradycardic at 25 to 39 beats per minute.
The next day a repeat head CT demonstrated acute ischemia of the left cerebellum mainly in the PICA distribution.

A head CT revealed hydrocephalus with dilation of the lateral ventricles including temporal horns and third ventricle, along with fourth ventricle compression and brain stem compression due to edema of a left cerebellar infarct.

After surgery, a head CT demonstrated a new hemorrhage and gas within the operative cavity along with an increased mass effect on the left side of the fourth ventricle which was completely effaced with moderate obstructive hydrocephalus.
The patient’s intracranial pressure (ICP) was found to be elevated and she had an external ventricular drain (EVD) placed for therapeutic drainage of her cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
She was able to perform a five-times-sit-to-stand test in 33 seconds with minimum assistance in the parallel bars.

By month ten, the patient had started to plateau with her functional level and was being prepared for discharge.
Overall she progressed in her independence for both basic and advanced ADL and transfers.
She resumed modified leisure activities such as working in her garden, painting and bike riding.

She continued to require support and supervision at home from family and hired assistance to ensure safety although she was able to function in her environment at the wheelchair level with little to no assistance.

Fourteen months after the initial infarcts, the patient was able to reside in her own home with her husband, ambulate, and stand with assistance and perform most activities of daily living with standby or set-up assistance.
This patient made significant progress toward safety and mobility and was able to return home despite the early discussion about a poor prognosis and a palliative care consultation.
Even after discharge from outpatient PT/OT, the patient’s spouse set up an unweighting harness for her home treadmill by installing asupport system in the ceiling of their living room.
The emergency room plan was to monitor orthostatic vital signs and aggressively hydrate overnight.
A PT treatment plan was established for balance retraining during her initial visits but subsequent medical events did not allow for PT interventions to be performed.
Based on her diagnosis and symptoms, the patient received an evaluation by SLP as well as PT and OT.
She demonstrated an initial score of three on the National Institute of Health Stroke Scale and was placed on the hospital stroke protocol.
In light of her poor prognosis, the patient received a palliative care consultation to assist in coordinating care and decision making 11 days after her fall and surgery.

The patient underwent a total of 14 months of PT and OT – six weeks in the intensive Care Unit (ICU), approximately 10 weeks in Inpatient Rehabilitation (IPR), and 41 weeks of outpatient rehabilitation.
The patient was in the ICU for a total of six weeks and received 19 visits of OT, 12 visits of PT, and 17 visits of SLP.
The OT sessions lasted 30 to 45 minutes while PT sessions lasted 30 minutes.
Occupational therapy was performed immediately prior to PT to optimize wakefulness and participation in early mobility activities.

After PT/OT treatment plans were established, they prescribed complimentary restorative aide services (trained technicians supervised by OTs and PTs who assist patients with exercises, general mobility and ROM) for a total of eight times while in the ICU.
Occupational therapy evaluation, interventions and outcomes: Three days after the initial fall and surgery, the patient was evaluated by OT.
Goals of OT were to increase environmental engagement and response to stimuli to begin early mobility with physical therapy.
Physical therapy evaluation, interventions and outcomes: Physical therapy treatments were initiated 30 days after the patient’s initial fall and eight days after OT was initiated in the ICU.
The physical therapist also provided a home exercise program and fall prevention education to the family and nursing.
During inpatient rehabilitation, the patient received a total of 54 visits of OT, 51 visits of PT, 47 visits of SLP and 22 visits of recreation therapy.
The patient was in the inpatient rehab setting for 10 weeks and consistently maintained the admission criteria for three hours per day averaging five to seven days per week.

Home adaptations included a wheelchair ramp and was discharged to home with a wheelchair, platform walker, shower chair, tub transfer bench and subsequently received outpatient PT and OT after a one week gap in treatment due to the holidays.

Upon initiation of outpatient PT and OT seventeen weeks after her fall and craniotomy surgery, the patient presented with decreased core strength requiring a specialized wheelchair for positioning and stability.
During outpatient rehabilitation, the patient received a total of 117 visits of OT, 115 visits of PT, and 110 visits of SLP over 41 weeks of rehabilitation.
Occupational therapy evaluation, interventions and outcomes: Occupational therapy was initiated three times a week for 45 to 60 minutes per session.

A re-evaluation was completed after the third month which provided evidence of an increase in control and strength for completion of modified ADLs and transfers with minimal to moderate assistance with perturbations 50% of the time.
Physical therapy evaluation, interventions and outcomes: Physical therapy was initiated in conjunction with OT and SLP, three times a week for 45 minute sessions each.
